messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

output:
# Why We're Funding a Developer Relations Team

Last quarter we watched a support ticket sit open for nine days. The customer had wired our webhook signing wrong, following a code sample from our own docs that had been stale since the v2 migration. They eventually gave up and switched to a competitor. Nobody on the team was assigned to notice.

That ticket is the argument for this hire, or rather these three hires. We are staffing a developer relations team starting in October.

The job is not conference talks. The first six months are docs triage, sample code that actually runs in CI, and someone whose full-time work is reading what developers say about us in places we don't control. Our API has grown by roughly 40 endpoints in eighteen months, and the documentation has been maintained by whoever shipped the endpoint, in the hour before they shipped it. That model got us here. It will not get us to ten thousand integrators.

We also want the feedback loop pointed inward. Engineers who build the API are poor judges of whether the API is usable, because they already know the answers. A developer relations team sits in the gap and reports back, with specifics: which error message sends people to Stack Overflow, which auth flow takes four attempts.

The budget comes out of paid acquisition. We spent a lot last year buying attention from developers who then hit our getting-started guide and bounced. Fixing the guide is cheaper.

We'll publish what we learn, including the parts that make us look bad.
